Neonates of the Anatolian lizard (Apathya cappadocica) emerge after an incubation period lasting approximately 90 days [ab = approximately 90 days] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a duration that aligns well with the developmental rates observed in other lacertids from similar montane environments. Upon hatching, these young individuals possess a wet body mass of about 1.3 grams [Wwb = about 1.3 grams], which represents a relatively modest starting size compared to the ultimate masses attained by adults. At this stage, the snout-to-vent length (SVL) of a hatchling is approximately 3.2 centimeters [Lb = approximately 3.2 centimeters], a value that underscores the considerable growth trajectory required to reach reproductive maturity. The initial feeding phase, commencing with the onset of exogenous feeding, is critical for the rapid accretion of somatic tissue, as the hatchling must more than double its structural size and increase its body mass by an order of magnitude over the subsequent months to survive its first winter.

In controlled laboratory conditions held at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the species exhibits a maximum reproductive rate equivalent to slightly more than eight offspring produced over a full year [Ri = eight offspring produced over a full year]. This modest annual output is achieved through the laying of relatively small clutches, with gravid females typically producing a single clutch per year containing approximately 8 eggs. The energetic demands of vitellogenesis and eggshell deposition in this oviparous adult are substantial, and the extended interval between successive reproductive events likely reflects the constraints imposed by the cool, seasonal climate of the Anatolian plateau. This life-history strategy, characterized by infrequent but defined reproductive bouts, contrasts with the higher frequency breeding observed in many lowland lacertids and is likely an adaptation to the short active season available for foraging and egg incubation.

Males of Apathya cappadocica ultimately attain a greater asymptotic snout-to-vent length than females, with the largest recorded individuals reaching 8.35 centimeters [Li = 8.35 centimeters], while adult females typically achieve a maximum SVL of 7.11 centimeters [Li = 7.11 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males being both longer and more robust, is a common feature within the genus and is frequently attributed to intrasexual selection for territory defense. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight for males, which peaks at approximately 23.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 23.6 grams], is substantially higher than the maximum recorded body mass for females of 14.6 grams [Wwi = 14.6 grams]. This differential growth pattern means that males invest more heavily in somatic development before diverting resources toward reproduction, a delay that is reflected in the timing of key life-history transitions.

Puberty in this saxicolous lizard is not reached until a considerable time after emergence from the egg, with individuals becoming sexually mature approximately 730 days after hatching [tp = approximately 730 days after hatching] when raised under a thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This protracted juvenile period is characteristic of a relatively slow life-history pace and likely correlates with the time required to accumulate sufficient energy reserves in a resource-limited environment. The interval from birth to reproductive maturity is further influenced by the necessity of attaining a minimum body size, particularly for females, who must achieve a sufficient pelvic aperture and body cavity volume to accommodate developing eggs. The onset of gonadal activation during this phase marks the transition from the pre-reproductive juvenile stage to the reproductively viable adult stage, after which individuals can participate in the annual breeding aggregations typical of the species.

Maximum longevity in Apathya cappadocica is estimated to be around 7 years [am = around 7 years] under captive conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], though field-based records suggest that free-living individuals may experience a slightly compressed lifespan due to predation and seasonal energy stress. This relatively extended lifespan for a small-bodied lacertid, combined with the delayed onset of puberty, suggests that the species follows a conservative life-history strategy favoring adult survival over high fecundity in any single season. The gradual process of senescence, characterized by a decline in locomotor performance and reproductive output, typically becomes evident after the fifth year. Natural mortality in the oldest individuals results from the progressive failure of physiological homeostasis, marking the completion of the species' life cycle. These demographic parameters place Apathya cappadocica among the slower-paced reptiles of the Palearctic region, with a generational turnover that buffers populations against short-term environmental fluctuations.
